name: Marco Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government; we don't sell anything or campaign. This is confidential, and you can give me your public answer separately from what you actually think. Tell me about a normal day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise four people who set sale prices and shelf notices for a large homewares chain. The shop teams send stock counts, we check the promotion calendar and I sign off what gets printed. I moved up from a shop role eight months ago and still sometimes approve a discount that leaves too little stock. I use AI every day to compare counts and draft notices, then my senior clerk checks my sums.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a display I planned actually work in a store, not just in a slide. I have a bachelor's degree, but I'm plainly still learning the manager's numbers. I'm 43; my partner Iris and I have a mortgage and children aged ten and fourteen. Iris works full time in a library, and between us we have four months of expenses saved. My pay is about normal for a manager here, and there are some other retail offices nearby, though I wouldn't assume they have a vacancy for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small tool could still catch price typos, and the rest would be the same scramble before a sale. I would have time to get better at managing the calendar. We have four months in the bank, so a bad promotion wouldn't make us miss the mortgage tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep checking the printed price against the shelf label. I'd tell Iris this picture leaves my job much as it is. I would still let the AI tool prepare the first stock comparison, because it saves a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, though I know my own mistakes are a bigger threat than the tool right now. Iris's library hours are steady, and our four months saved makes the mortgage feel manageable. I don't want to be the manager who confuses a neat report with goods on a shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this Friday I'd ask the senior clerk to check the three largest price changes with me before any signs print. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep the same team and use the existing AI comparison only for a first pass, checking a store count myself. I'd put 100 each month from our usual pay into the emergency account while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the family bills and a little embarrassed about how many corrections I still need. The quiet picture gives me practice time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the clerk catch last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lamp was marked as having thirty in stock, but twenty were already reserved for online orders. I'd signed a price drop before she showed me the reserved column. We stopped the sign before any shop had to apologise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put more in cash if the mortgage feels manageable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months isn't forever, and one of our children will need school trips paid for soon. A small regular transfer is easier than a panicked cut later. I won't promise 100 in a month when the car needs a repair.

say: I'd tell staff to check **printed prices** against shelf labels before each sale.
I'd tell Iris the AI **first comparison** saves minutes while the job stays much the same.
think: My **own pricing mistakes** worry me more than modest AI change.
Four months saved and **Iris's steady hours** make our bills feel manageable.
do: Check the **three largest price changes** with the senior clerk before printing.
Keep the **existing AI comparison** as a first pass, then check store counts.
Transfer **100 monthly** to emergency cash while both wages continue, unless the car needs repair.
feel: I feel **calm** about bills, though I am embarrassed by needed corrections.
S0.quote: I don't want to be the manager who confuses a neat report with goods on a shelf.
fieldNote: The **reserved lamp stock** shows why he still relies on the senior clerk's checks.
His **four-month reserve** and Iris's wage steady the household in a mild scenario.
He already uses AI daily and keeps its **first-pass role**, rather than adding a new tool.

steps.text: Check the three largest price changes with the senior clerk before printing
Transfer 100 monthly while both wages continue, unless the car needs repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing signs, checking stock, planning discounts and answering stores are our full week. Stronger AI could do those tasks faster and leave one manager checking a whole region. The shops still need people putting goods on shelves, but that is not the job my four staff and I have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the director to test the system on a real short-stock sale before promising savings. I'd tell my team what the trial finds, including where it gets a price wrong. I wouldn't sell them a cheerful story about all five posts staying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be the manager cut, because I'm still learning and the senior clerk knows more about the numbers. My daily use of AI gives me a chance to run a trial, but it doesn't make me irreplaceable. Iris's wage and our savings would cover the mortgage for a while, not indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask for a paid six-week pilot on last year's promotions and learn the system's stock limits with my clerk. If the director approves a rollout, I'd automate only the first draft of sale notices and keep a person checking the printed price against actual stock. I'd also check the posted jobs at two nearby retail offices while I have a wage, without treating an advert as an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing my seat, even as I want to test the new tool. The difference between a trial and a layoff is one budget meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test from last year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the lamp sale we nearly got wrong and ask whether the tool subtracts online reservations before it suggests a price. If it misses that, the printed sign waits. I could show the director a number rather than just say I feel uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the senior clerk you might be cut instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, privately. She'd be angry if I hid behind my title, and she'd be right. I would ask for the staffing plan in writing for both of us.

say: I'd ask for a **real short-stock test** before claiming savings.
I'd tell the team when a trial finds **wrong prices** and seek a written staffing plan.
think: I could be the **manager cut** because my clerk knows the numbers better.
Daily AI use offers a trial role, but **Iris's wage and savings** cannot replace mine indefinitely.
do: Run a **six-week paid pilot** if the director approves it.
Learn **stock-limit settings** with the senior clerk before automating first drafts.
Check **two nearby retail offices** for posted jobs while still paid.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own post despite curiosity about the tool.
S1.quote: The difference between a trial and a layoff is one budget meeting.
fieldNote: He names **his own weak numbers** rather than assuming AI skill protects his manager title.
The pilot would test **online reservations** and keep a person checking printed prices.
He looks at **posted vacancies**, without assuming a nearby office has an open job.

steps.text: Learn the system stock limits with the senior clerk during an approved pilot
Automate first sale-notice drafts only if the director approves rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 a full thinking system could choose prices, check stock and write better signs than our office. A shop assistant may still hang the sign and carry a lamp until robots around 2031, but that isn't an automatic place for me. My role is mostly screen decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff the date in the card and ask for a written notice period and real vacancies. I'd tell Iris our four months of savings cover a short search, not a career change on faith. In public I'd say a company should pay for a worker to try another role before closing the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the promotion manager role to go around 2028. Iris's library pay would cover only part of our mortgage and essentials, so I would watch our reserve shrink each month. The nearby retail offices might automate their pricing too; I cannot count them as safe jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the store director for a paid two-day trial putting up displays and counting damaged goods, with training and shift cover. I'd stop the planned spring trip before paying the deposit and keep that money in cash. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk post goes, I'd apply for a posted store-display job only if its pay plus Iris's covers mortgage, food and child care; otherwise I'd search the nearby employers while using the four-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed at losing the larger wage. Four months is time to act, but it is not enough to try three bad jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would display work really last to 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical lifting and fitting may, while the display plan and stock report could go to AGI in 2028. I would need the store to pay for actual hands-on duties, not a new title with the same desk work. I can't promise the post would still exist after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for retraining yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before seeing the wage and a vacancy. We could pay for a short course, but the mortgage comes first. I want a paid trial to learn whether I can do eight hours on the shop floor at 43.

say: I'd ask for **written notice and vacancies** before the promotion office closes.
I'd tell Iris our savings buy a **short search**, not a guaranteed new career.
think: I expect my **promotion role to end** around 2028.
Iris's pay covers only **part of the bills**, so our reserve would fall monthly.
do: Request a **paid display trial** with training and shift cover now.
Cancel the **spring trip** before its deposit and keep the money in cash.
Apply after 2028 only for **posted physical store work** whose combined pay covers family bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected salary loss and a four-month deadline on cash.
S2.quote: Four months is time to act, but it is not enough to try three bad jobs.
fieldNote: He expects **2028 desk loss**, while physical display work may last until robots around 2031.
The paid trial requires **shift cover and training**, and any job needs enough combined pay for essentials.
His daily AI use does not solve the **family wage gap** after a layoff.

steps.text: Complete a paid two-day display trial if training and shift cover are provided
Cancel the spring trip before paying its deposit
Apply for posted display work only if combined wages cover mortgage, food and child care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me find out whether I can do shop work and make the mortgage numbers add up before the office faces AGI in 2031. The physical display work faces robots around 2034. I might be able to move early, but a store would still have to offer paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we have time to ask for paid rotations, not just online courses. I'd say to Iris we should keep four months of expenses untouched while I test a lower wage. I wouldn't tell anyone that shop work is forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be earning in a store by 2031 if the company has a real opening, but its plans and ordering will change then too. A slower deadline lets me learn without resigning first. I still worry my manager pay would fall before we've reduced the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd request one paid store-display day each month and, if approved, work those days with a trained installer. I'd put 150 monthly into a separate cash account while both wages cover mortgage and food, aiming for a buffer above our current four months. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd take a posted physical display position only if its pay with Iris's covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'd keep searching the other retail offices with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, with more control than in the two-year picture. The mortgage still turns a smaller wage into a real question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from the installer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to secure a heavy shelf unit without hiding its safety clips and how to count what is actually in the aisle. A design file won't show a loose bracket. I would need supervision before being trusted to sign off a display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your director refuses paid days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my current role and ask one of the other chains about a real opening, not sign up for an unpaid course. My children need me home on school nights. I can't turn a mortgage into a hobby project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I will be 53, and our children will be twenty and twenty-four. We might have a smaller mortgage by then, but I won't count on that today. The promotion desk faces AGI in 2036, and robots capable of physical shop work arrive around 2039, so even a store move has a time limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger managers to learn the numbers behind a sale, not only the tool. I'd tell our company to offer paid store rotations before any big desk cuts. A decade is useful if wages keep coming while people learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use this job for several more years, build cash and get good at both prices and physical displays. I don't expect a title to protect my desk in 2036. With Iris's steady wage and more savings, I might choose a lower-paid store role without risking the mortgage, if a real one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for a paid two-day store rotation each month, and if approved I'd complete stock and display checks alongside a qualified worker. I'd keep sending 200 monthly into cash after the mortgage and school bills are paid, aiming for six months of expenses by 2032. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd apply for a posted store role only if its physical duties and combined wages still fit; otherwise I'd use the cash cushion to search while robots remain about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point, but not frantic. Ten years gives me time to correct my weak spots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the savings target misses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then six months may take longer; I won't make a number up by skipping the children's needs. The first transfer comes after the mortgage. We can review the plan when one of them finishes school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep learning prices if AI does them by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I need to manage the team and judge mistakes while I'm still paid to do it. That knowledge may help me run a pilot or explain a bad sign to a shop, but I don't think it is a permanent shield. I want to be useful now as well as prepared later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A tool that makes every pricing call better than I do could remove the promotion work before I've found another post. A dated notice, a paid trial doing physical store displays and an actual opening at wages we can live on would help. Four months saved buys time, not a new manager job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who goes to the shop when a bright sale sign promises a lamp that's already gone. The shop assistant gets the shouting, while the office blames a stock number. I want to see the empty shelf before I call the promotion a success.

headlineQuote: I want to see the empty shelf before I call the promotion a success.
portrait: Marco, **43**, became a junior promotions manager at a large homewares chain and checks prices and signs with four staff.
He uses **AI daily** but still needs a senior clerk to catch stock and discount errors after only eight months in management.
He and Iris have **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with four months saved on manager and library wages.
He would test **paid store-display work** if a real opening exists, recognising thinking work changes before physical shop tasks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the promotion office before he finds another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated notice** and a paid trial doing physical displays while his office wage continues.
An **actual store opening** with wages that cover the family mortgage and essentials.
